newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu against recapturing West Bank towns.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu against recapturing West Bank towns.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, trying to soften what the PLO called empty threats by his defence chief, said on Thursday Israel was not interested in retaking Palestinian-ruled West Bank towns.
Earlier comments by Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai that Israel would have "no difficulty" recapturing the towns, but that it did not want to send in troops, angered Palestinians.

In the West Bank town of Hebron, Israeli troops wounded seven Palestinians with rubber bullets in the latest round of clashes, witnesses said. Israeli soldiers and settlers killed three Palestinians in Hebron on Tuesday.

"It is true that we have the capability to return to the towns but we are not interested, as the defence minister rightly said, of going with this option," Netanyahu told reporters in Netherlands in broadcast remarks.
"We are searching for another option, primarily stopping violence and terror and continuing the peace process between us and the Palestinians to achieve real peace," he said.

Street battles have flared nearly every day in the West Bank since Netanyahu sent bulldozers on March 18 to start work on a Jewish settlement on an Arab East Jerusalem hill called Har Homa in Hebrew and Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic.

In Washington, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright warned in a speech to the American Society of Newspaper Editors of an "unpredictable and dangerous" Middle East situation as PLO officials arrived for talks on reviving the peace process.

Arab-Israeli gains of recent years were threatened and the people of the region had again become victims of confrontation and violence, Albright said in her most gloomy assessment so far of peace prospects in the region.
"The reason is that Arabs and Israelis alike have begun to lose faith in one another. The Oslo process and the working partnership between Israelis and Palestinians have broken down," she said.
Albright was later to meet top Palestinian negotiators Saeb Erekat and Mahmoud Abbas. The two men went to the State Department for talks with Middle East envoy Dennis Ross.
In The Hague, Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok said the European Union wants to share in Middle East peace diplomacy but sees its role as supplementary to that of the United States.
"The European Union chooses a balanced approach. We want to play a role in the talks in addition to the Americans, not instead of the Americans," he told a news conference with Netanyahu.
Speaking to troops on the Golan Heights, Mordechai said in reply to a question: "There would be no difficulty recapturing Hebron or any other city but we don't want to do that."
He was referring to eight Palestinian towns handed over to self-rule since a landmark 1993 peace agreement.
Ahmed Abdel-Rahman, secretary-general of the Palestinian Authority, said: "We wish Mr Mordechai would stop issuing such empty threats. Entering (Palestinian cities) would not be easy."
In what he described as "localised" security cooperation, Netanyahu said Palestinian security forces had helped Israel discover the body of an Israeli soldier missing since September.
Israeli troops in the West Bank on Thursday found Sergeant Sharon Edri's corpse buried in the home village of a Moslem suicide bomber who blew up a Tel Aviv cafe last month.
The military said a six-member squad of the militant Moslem group Hamas was responsible for his kidnapping and killing in central Israel and the deaths of 10 other Israelis since 1996.

"In the last part of the operation (to find Edri)...the Palestinian Authority arrested two members of the squad and through their arrest we were able to determine finally the place where Edri was buried," Netanyahu said.

But the right-wing Israeli leader, who has conditioned a return to peace talks with the Palestinians on a PLO crackdown on Moslem militants, said it had yet to start cooperating fully with Israel on stopping "terrorism".

PLO officials said Palestinian security chiefs refused a request by U.S. Central Intelligence Agency and Israeli security officials at a secret meeting attended by President Yasser Arafat in Gaza on Tuesday to restore security ties with Israel.
